q: An investor has a portfolio worth ₹50 lakh with beta 1.2. To hedge with Nifty futures (price 25,000, lot size 25), the number of contracts to short is approximately:
e: Hedge ratio = (β × Portfolio value) / (Future price × Lot size) = (1.2 × 50,00,000) / (25,000 × 25) = 60,00,000 / 6,25,000 = 9.6 ≈ 10 contracts.

q: A long straddle is constructed by:
o: Buying a call and selling a put at the same strike
Buying a call and a put at the same strike and same expiry
Selling a call and a put at the same strike
Buying calls at two different strikes
e: Long straddle = long call + long put at the SAME strike, SAME expiry. Profitable if the underlying moves significantly in either direction beyond X ± total premium.

q: A long strangle differs from a long straddle in that:
o: The two legs use different strikes
e: Strangle uses an OTM call and an OTM put — different strikes, same expiry. It's cheaper than a straddle but needs a bigger move to break even.
Covered call = long stock + short out-of-the-money call. The investor caps upside at the strike but earns premium income; protection on downside is limited to the premium.

q: A 'protective put' strategy is suitable for an investor who:
o: Holds a long stock position and wants downside protection
Wants to speculate on a stock decline
e: Protective put = long stock + long put. The put acts as insurance — limiting downside to (Spot − Strike + Premium), while keeping unlimited upside (less the premium paid).

o: Long stock + long put + short call
Long stock + long call + short put
e: Collar = long stock + long OTM put + short OTM call. Caps both downside (via the put) and upside (via the short call). Often near-zero net cost when premiums offset.

q: If futures price exceeds the fair value, the appropriate arbitrage is:
e: Cash-and-carry: when futures > fair value, borrow at r, buy the spot, sell the overpriced futures, deliver into the futures at expiry. Risk-free profit = futures − fair value (less costs).

q: A trader expects high volatility in Nifty before earnings but is unsure of direction. The best strategy is:
e: Long straddle or strangle profits from large moves in either direction. Both gain when implied volatility rises (positive vega) and when the underlying moves enough to cross the BEPs.

q: A long butterfly spread is constructed using:
o: Three different strikes (1 ITM long, 2 ATM short, 1 OTM long)
e: Long butterfly: long 1 ITM call + short 2 ATM calls + long 1 OTM call (or all puts). Profits if the underlying stays near the middle strike at expiry — bets on low movement.

q: Delta-hedging an option position aims to:
e: Delta-hedging neutralises the directional exposure (delta = 0) by holding offsetting units of the underlying. Gamma re-introduces directionality as spot moves, requiring continuous re-hedging.

q: If put-call parity is violated such that C − P > S − X × e^(−r × t), an arbitrageur should:
o: Sell the call, buy the put, buy the stock
Buy the call, sell the put, sell the stock
e: If LHS > RHS, the call is relatively expensive and the put is relatively cheap. Sell call, buy put, buy stock (synthesised at strike via borrowing), lock in the spread.

q: An investor who is bullish on a stock but only mildly should consider a:
e: Bull call spread (long lower-strike call + short higher-strike call) gives bullish exposure with lower premium outlay vs a naked long call. Caps upside at the higher strike but reduces the breakeven.
